title: Single-Minded Buddha-Recitation, Not Distracted Recitation
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Single-mindedness is the key to correct practice in the Pure Land school.

inline.s: Single-mindedness is the key to correct practice in the Pure Land school.
Master Shandao, the manifestation of Amitābha Buddha, taught:
Reciting scriptures, contemplation, bowing to the Buddha, Buddha-recitation, and praise and offerings—
all must be done with a single mind; only then is it the correct practice.
Single-minded Buddha-recitation accords with the vow of Amitābha Buddha,
whereas distracted recitation contradicts the vow of Amitābha Buddha.
“The mouth recites Amitābha while the mind is far astray
(distracted recitation)
; though you shout your throat to hoarseness, it is all in vain.”
Do away with the bad habit of distracted recitation,
and cultivate the good habit of single-minded recitation, until habit becomes nature.
Success or failure hangs on this very step!
This is the field where Buddhas are chosen; with a single mind you pass the exam and return.
[While the mouth recites Amitābha the mind is scattered; though you shout your throat hoarse it is all in vain]—these are the heartfelt words of Master Hanshan, who was awakened to the great Way!
Q: What is mind-gathering Buddha-recitation? How does it compare with single-minded Buddha-recitation?

A: To gather the mind means to make the mind focus upon a single object, without scattering and without dullness. Therefore, mind-gathering Buddha-recitation is single-minded Buddha-recitation. Mind-gathering recitation (single-minded recitation) is extremely important,
for it is the Way that is fixed and unalterable.
On this, Master Yinguang taught:
“Gathering the mind in Buddha-recitation
is the Way that is fixed and unalterable.
(In Collected Writings of Master Yinguang,
First Letter in Reply to Layman Liu Guanshan.) He further taught:
“If the six faculties are not gathered, though one recites the Buddha, deluded thoughts still fly wildly in the mind,
and real benefit is hard to gain.
(In Collected Writings of Master Yinguang,
Letter in Reply to Master Huanxiu.) Master Daochuo taught:
“The wise diligently gather the mind, so at the end of life their thoughts do not scatter
(and so they accomplish right mindfulness at death and are reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)
; but one who does not practice single-minded focus will surely be scattered at death,
(and so they fail to accomplish right mindfulness at death and instead continue to revolve through the six realms)
(From The Collection of Peace and Bliss, the Anle Ji.)
Q: In reciting the Buddha's name, should one practice single-minded recitation or distracted recitation?
A: One should recite single-mindedly; distracted recitation is wrong.
For the condition of rebirth is ten consecutive thoughts at the moment of death
(see
The Conditions for Rebirth

Single-minded recitation is precisely in order to accomplish those ten consecutive thoughts at death, which distracted recitation cannot do. Master Daochuo taught: if one recites distractedly in daily life, how can one then accomplish ten consecutive thoughts at the end of life? Therefore the wise diligently gather the mind and recite single-mindedly. (The original text:
“The wise diligently gather the mind, so at the end of life their thoughts do not scatter; but one who does not practice single-minded focus will surely be scattered at death.”
) See
Master Daochuo's Pure Land Teaching
. The patriarchs and great masters of all ages have taught in just this way. For instance, Master Yinguang taught:
Distracted recitation rarely attains rebirth; single-minded recitation surely attains rebirth.
(In Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, Letter in Reply to Layman Chen Xizhou.)
Master Shandao, the manifestation of Amitābha Buddha, also earnestly instructed: one must recite single-mindedly. These are the very words of Amitābha Buddha!
Master Shandao taught:
With a single mind,
recite only the name of Amitābha—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, regardless of the length of time,
never letting go from thought to thought
—such a person is said to be in the karma of right and settled concentration,
because it accords with that Buddha's vow.
This
is the teaching of Master Shandao in the Four-Fascicle Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra,
which explains precisely how to recite the Buddha

Translation: Reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha single-mindedly—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, regardless of the length of time, never letting go from thought to thought—is called the karma of right and settled concentration, because it accords with the vow of Amitābha Buddha.
[Single-mindedness.] Master Tanluan taught in his Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth: single-mindedness means thought following upon thought, with no other thought mixed in. (See
Master Tanluan's Pure Land Teaching

) [Never letting go from thought to thought.] Every single thought is the name of Amitābha. [Right and settled concentration.] Correct meditation—the body and mind pure and clear, without scattering—is called "right and settled concentration." [Karma.] The activities of body, speech, and mind. [Because it accords with that Buddha's vow.] "Reciting the name of Amitābha single-mindedly—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, regardless of the length of time, never letting go from thought to thought"—this is because it accords with the vow of Amitābha Buddha.
Master Shandao is the incarnation of Amitābha; his words are the words of Amitābha Buddha. From this we know that when sentient beings
recite single-mindedly, never letting go from thought to thought,
this accords with the vow of Buddha Amitābha. Then
distracted recitation on the other hand defies the vow of Amitābha Buddha!
[Distracted recitation.] The mouth recites the Buddha's name while the mind thinks of other things.
As for distracted recitation,
Master Hanshan taught in his Song of Wasted Effort:
The mouth recites Amitābha while the mind is scattered; though you shout your throat hoarse, it is all in vain.”
[Song of Wasted Effort.] “

fei” means to spend time and energy, while “xian” means useless, a waste of effort. Feixian means spending time and energy with no real result—what is commonly called doing useless work. In the Song of Wasted Effort, Master Hanshan points out the common pitfalls of wasted effort in practice, and how to escape them.
(See
The Annotated Song of Wasted Effort
Now I transcribe and annotate this teaching of Master Hanshan as follows:

[Reciting the Buddha is easy, but a true believing heart is rare; when mouth and mind are not at one, all the practice is but wasted effort. The mouth recites Amitābha while the mind is far astray; though you shout until your throat is hoarse, it is all in vain.]

Reciting the Buddha is easy, but a heart of genuine sincerity is hard; when the mouth and mind are not at one (the heart not truly sincere: while the mouth recites the Buddha, the mind thinks of other things) it is always in vain (all wasted effort); while the mouth recites Amitābha Buddha, the mind thinks of other things, and even if you shout until your throat is hoarse it is to no avail.

[Believing heart.] A heart of genuine sincerity; when the mouth and mind are not at one, it is false. So the next line goes: "when mouth and mind are not at one, it is always in vain (all wasted effort)." Here "faith" does not mean the faith of faith, vow, and practice, but rather sincerity.
For example, the "faithful wind" is the wind that comes as promised each year when its season arrives—a wind of true reliability.

[Sincerity.] To be honest and not to deceive. [Though you shout your throat hoarse it is all in vain.] Because "the mouth recites Amitābha while the mind is scattered (distracted recitation)" cannot accomplish the ten consecutive thoughts at death (the minimum requirement for rebirth; see The Conditions for Rebirth), one does not attain rebirth—all the effort is wasted.
Here Master Hanshan hits the mark in a single stroke:
“The mouth recites Amitābha while the mind is scattered
(distracted recitation)
; though you shout your throat hoarse, it is all in vain.”
Single-mindedness

—this is the key to correct practice in the Pure Land school. Master Shandao, the manifestation of Amitābha Buddha, taught: in reciting scriptures, in contemplation, in bowing to the Buddha, in Buddha-recitation, and in praise and offerings, one must
be single-minded
; only then is it the correct practice.
Master Shandao also said:

“Now practice is of two kinds: the first is the correct practice; the second is the mixed practice. By the correct practice is meant one who practices exclusively in accordance with the rebirth scriptures—this is called the correct practice. What is this?
Single-mindedly
reciting only this Contemplation Sutra, the Amitābha Sutra, the Immeasurable Life Sutra, and so forth;
single-mindedly
concentrating thought, contemplation, and recollection on the majestic adornments of the two rewards of that Land. If one bows, then
single-mindedly
bow only to that Buddha; if one recites with the mouth, then
single-mindedly
recite only that Buddha's name; if one offers praise and offerings, then
single-mindedly
praise and make offerings only to that Buddha.
This is called the correct
(this is the correct practice)
(From the Four-Fascicle Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra.)
[Rebirth scriptures.] These are the three Pure Land scriptures: the Immeasurable Life Sutra, the Contemplation Sutra on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, and the Amitābha Sutra.

[The adornments of the two rewards.] The adornments of the dependent and the proper reward. [Dependent and proper.] The dependent reward and the proper reward. The dependent reward: the retribution one relies upon for dwelling, such as the land and earth, houses and utensils—in other words, one's living environment. The proper reward: the body and mind of the Buddhas and of sentient beings—the very substance of retribution drawn forth by past karmic causes. The proper rewards of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss are two: first, the adornment of the main subject, that is, Amitābha Buddha (the Buddha of Immeasurable Life); second, the adornment of the host of sages, that is, the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and devas of the Western Land. (See the Contemplation Sutra on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life.)
Single-minded Buddha-recitation is supremely excellent.
For when one recites single-mindedly, the three studies of precepts, concentration, and wisdom are all present:

Precepts guard against wrongdoing: if one can recite single-mindedly, then no evil enters—this is precepts. Concentration removes scattering: if one recites single-mindedly, the mind does not grasp at anything else—this is concentration. Wisdom is clear illumination: if one contemplates the Buddha's name so that every word is distinct, and also perceives that both the one who recites and the one recited are ungraspable—this is wisdom. Therefore single-minded recitation is itself precepts, concentration, and wisdom.

[The three studies.] The study of precepts, the study of concentration, and the study of wisdom. Precepts are the prohibitions, expounded in the vinaya-piṭaka, that prevent people from creating all evil karma of body, speech, and mind; concentration is meditative absorption, expounded in the sūtra-piṭaka, that enables people to still reflection and clarify the mind; wisdom is prajñā, expounded in the śāstra-piṭaka, that enables people to discover truth and cut off ignorance. By cultivating these three studies, one gains concentration from precepts and develops wisdom from concentration, and finally attains the undefiled fruit of the Way; hence the three studies are also called "the three undefiled studies."
For when one recites single-mindedly, the six pāramitās and the myriad practices are all complete:

Reciting single-mindedly, all conditions naturally fall away—this is the pāramitā of giving; reciting single-mindedly, all evils naturally cease—this is the pāramitā of keeping precepts; reciting single-mindedly, the mind naturally becomes gentle—this is the pāramitā of patience; reciting single-mindedly, one never falls back—this is the pāramitā of vigor; reciting single-mindedly, no other thoughts arise—this is the pāramitā of meditation; reciting single-mindedly, right mindfulness is clear—this is the pāramitā of prajñā. Extending this to all methods of practice, single-minded recitation fulfills the myriad practices.

[The six pāramitās.] Six methods for crossing from this shore of birth-and-death and suffering to the farther shore of nirvāṇa's bliss, namely giving, keeping precepts, patience, vigor, meditation, and prajñā. Giving crosses over miserliness and greed; keeping precepts crosses over transgression; patience crosses over anger; vigor crosses over indolence; meditation crosses over scattering; prajñā crosses over ignorance. [The six pāramitās and the myriad practices.] The Treatise on the Bodhi Mind says:
“Having further passed through three asaṃkhyeya kalpas
(three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas)
, practicing the six pāramitās and the myriad practices, all completely fulfilled, one then realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.”
Therefore single-minded Buddha-recitation is a gateway of great bliss and great liberation. Let go of all conditions and recite single-mindedly, and you attain great freedom.
Master Shandao, the manifestation of Amitābha Buddha, taught:
With a single mind
reciting only the name of Amitābha—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, regardless of the length of time,
never letting go from thought to thought
(each thought never drawn away by deluded thoughts)
—such a person is said to be
in the karma of right and settled concentration,
because it accords with that Buddha's
(Amitābha Buddha)
vow.
As for
single-minded recitation, Master Shandao further taught in his The Two Practices of Pure Karma: the Special and the Mixed:
It is precisely because calling the name is easy
that continuous recitation brings rebirth.
If one can
continue from thought to thought,
throughout life until the very end
for one who does so,
, of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred.
May all people reflect well on this: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, one must
stir the mind vigorously and restrain oneself
never desisting day or night
; when the former thought ends the life, the latter thought is at once born.
Forever enjoying the unconditioned Dharma-bliss, even attaining Buddhahood—how joyous is that!
The "thought after thought continuing" taught here has the same meaning as the "single-mindedly holding the name, never letting go from thought to thought" taught earlier;
it specifically explains how reciting the Buddha brings rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Master
Yinguang, the manifestation of Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, praised this teaching greatly, saying:

“Master Shandao is the incarnation of Amitābha, endowed with great transcendental powers and great wisdom. In his grand exposition of the Pure Land, he does not favor the mysterious and subtle, but only teaches people to practice with genuine, practical plainness.
As for the Two Practices: the Special and the Mixed that he set forth, its benefit is boundless.
(In Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, Letter to a Layman of Yongjia and His Brothers.) Now I annotate this as follows:
It is precisely because calling the name is easy,
that continuous recitation brings rebirth.
If one can
continue from thought to thought,
throughout life until the very end,
for one
a person who thus practices throughout his whole life
, of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred.]
Precisely because reciting the name is easier to accomplish than contemplation by visualization,
as long as at the moment of death one keeps the thought of recitation continuing,
(not broken by deluded thoughts)
, one immediately attains rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
If one's thought of recitation continues unbroken, then for one who thus practices throughout life—of ten people, all ten are reborn; of a hundred people, all a hundred.
[Continuous recitation brings rebirth.]
“Continuous recitation brings rebirth” means:
at the moment of death, when the thought of recitation continues unbroken
(not broken by deluded thoughts)
, one is born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Here "continuing" means the thought of recitation following upon thought, with no deluded thought mingled in between (if a deluded thought is mingled in, it is no longer continuous). One must never mistake the word "continuous" here for a mere verbal continuity of the Buddha's name (while deluded thoughts are mixed in the mind). As the saying goes, a hairbreadth of error leads to a thousand miles of wrong. [Thought after thought continuing, throughout life until the end.] Because at the moment of death an unbroken thought of recitation brings rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one must thus practice throughout life,
making the thought of recitation continuous until habit becomes nature

. In this way one is sure to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss—of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred. [Accumulated habit becomes nature.] This means that through repeated practice, the continuity of the thought of recitation becomes instinctive, which is what is commonly called "habit becomes nature."
[May all people reflect well on this: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, one must stir the mind vigorously and restrain oneself, never desisting day or night.]
May
all people
reflect well on this: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying,
they must all
earnestly
stir themselves and restrain themselves,
never letting the thought-to-thought recitation stop day or night.

[Stirring the mind vigorously and restraining oneself.] "Stirring the mind" means rousing one's mind to do what ought to be done; "restraining oneself" means curbing oneself from doing what ought not to be done. These four characters are a mighty weapon for overcoming difficulties and sweeping away obstacles.
[Never desisting day or night.] Do not let the thought-to-thought recitation stop day or night.
[When the former thought ends the life, the latter thought is at once born. Forever enjoying the unconditioned Dharma-bliss, even attaining Buddhahood—how joyous is that!]
Practicing in this way,
when the former thought ends the life, the latter thought is at once born
in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Forever enjoying the unconditioned Dharma-bliss, even attaining Buddhahood—how joyous is that!

[When the former thought ends the life, the latter thought is at once born.] This means: because the thought of recitation is unbroken, the final thought at death is necessarily a thought of recitation,
and immediately after that final thought
one is born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Q: There is a saying: "Even though one recites distractedly, as long as faith and vow are complete, one will still certainly be reborn." Is this saying correct?

A: The Buddha and the patriarchs have repeatedly taught us to recite single-mindedly, and have repeatedly urged us to practice as they have said. Therefore, one whose faith and vow are complete will certainly practice as instructed and recite single-mindedly. One who recites distractedly does so because he fears difficulty and hardship, or is lazy and remiss, and so acts against the teaching of the Buddha and the patriarchs—
this is precisely the concrete expression of faith that is not true and a vow that is not earnest.
Therefore, one who recites distractedly certainly does not have complete faith and vow.

"Even though one recites distractedly, as long as faith and vow are complete" means: reciting distractedly while having complete faith and vow. Yet this situation of "reciting distractedly while having complete faith and vow"
simply does not exist; it is a false proposition.
, just as there is no brave warrior who cowers before the enemy on the battlefield. Since such a situation does not exist, how can one even speak of rebirth or no rebirth? Therefore,
"Even though one recites distractedly, as long as faith and vow are complete, one will still certainly be reborn" is fundamentally a fallacy.
[False proposition.] A proposition that is not true. [Proposition.] A declarative sentence that expresses a judgment.
Q: Why is it said that
the situation of "reciting distractedly while having complete faith and vow" simply does not exist?
A:
Master Yongming, the manifestation of Amitābha Buddha, taught:
“If
words and deeds do not correspond
(words and deeds do not match)
, with the power of faith slight and weak,
with no heart of thought-after-thought recitation but a mind of repeated interruption
(the thought of recitation broken by deluded thoughts)
—such a person,
relying on this indolence
(depending on this lazy practice)
, hoping for rebirth at death
(wishing to be reborn at the end of life)
, is but covered by karmic obstacles
(but hindered by karmic hindrances)
, and fearing that it is hard to meet a good friend
(fearing it hard to encounter a good teacher who can help him accomplish right mindfulness at death)
, when wind and fire press upon him,
right mindfulness is not accomplished.
(being unable to accomplish right mindfulness at death—the ten consecutive thoughts at the end of life—and therefore not attaining rebirth)
If one wishes
to accomplish the ten thoughts at death,
one should prepare the crossing beforehand, accumulate merit, and dedicate it to this moment
(dedicating it to the moment of death)
, with no shortfall in thought after thought
(accomplishing thought-after-thought continuity)
, then there is nothing to worry about.”
(From The Compendium of the Myriad Good Deeds Returning to One, the Wanshan Tonggui Ji.)

[Master Yongming, the manifestation of Amitābha Buddha.] Master Yongming is the manifestation of Amitābha Buddha, and so his birthday on the seventeenth day of the eleventh lunar month is observed as the birthday of Amitābha Buddha. Concerning Master Yongming, Master Yinguang praised:
“Master Yongming is the incarnation of Amitābha Buddha. With great compassion and great mercy, he opens and transforms sentient beings.”

(In Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, Dharma Words Spoken at the World Buddhist Laymen's Association.) Therefore, the words of Master Yongming are as if spoken by Amitābha Buddha in person. [Words and deeds do not correspond.] Words and deeds do not match. With the mouth one claims true faith and an earnest vow, but in actual action the faith is not true and the vow not earnest: one fears difficulty and hardship, and is lazy and remiss. So Master Yongming's next line is:
“The power of faith is slight and weak.”
And he rebukes, saying:
“Relying on this indolence.”
[Accomplishing the ten thoughts at death.] Accomplishing the ten consecutive thoughts at the end of life.
(See
The Eighteenth Vow
) [Preparing the crossing beforehand.] "Crossing" means a ferry and a bridge. "Preparing the crossing beforehand" means making ready in advance.
In this teaching,
"no heart of thought-after-thought recitation but a mind of repeated interruption"
is distracted recitation. Why does one recite distractedly? Master Yongming taught that this is because
"words and deeds do not correspond, and the power of faith is slight and weak,"
that is to say,
faith and vow are not true and earnest.
Moreover, Master Yongming rebukes distracted recitation as
"relying on this indolence,"
and its result is
"right mindfulness is not accomplished,"
and rebirth is not attained.
Therefore,
the situation of "reciting distractedly while having complete faith and vow" simply does not exist.
Moreover, the result of distracted recitation
is:
right mindfulness is not accomplished at death, and rebirth is not attained.
Reciters of the Buddha must firmly remember the earnest teaching of the World-Honored One in the Sutra of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, and always remind themselves:
Though one toils diligently in this one life,
in an instant one is thereafter born in the Land of Immeasurable Life,
with joy beyond measure.

Single-minded recitation is in fact not difficult. In this world, no matter which skill one learns, one must follow the correct method and practice with perseverance and resolve before one can master it—for example, learning to play the piano, playing basketball, and so on. By comparison, mastering single-minded recitation is far easier than learning to play the piano, and its meaning and worth are beyond words. Once you have mastered the method of single-minded recitation, recite with it each day, and over time skill naturally grows into mastery. Then what need is there to fret that you cannot be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss at the end of life?

To be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and so put an end to birth-and-death and escape the cycle of rebirth is the foremost affair of this life, and it must be accomplished with perseverance and resolve. Always remind yourself: once reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, you will have a vajra body like that of Nārāyaṇa, forever free from old age, sickness, suffering, and death, receiving only all manner of bliss until you attain Buddhahood. In this cultivation, what difficulty remains that cannot be overcome?
There are two kinds of people in the world: dreamers and doers (
Dreamer and Doer

). Dreamers are good at talking, imagining, longing, and even planning to do great things; but doers go and do! Right now you are a dreamer, and it seems that no matter how hard you try, you cannot bring yourself to accomplish those things you know you should, or could, do. But never mind—you can still turn yourself into a doer.” —
Habit and Success
Q: How does one accomplish single-minded recitation?
A: The following books and articles all set forth specific methods of single-minded recitation, and you may choose according to your own circumstances. They are:
Investigating and Contemplating Buddha-Recitation
Aware Buddha-Recitation
The Essence of Breath Buddha-Recitation
Ten Thoughts at Death, Continuous Recitation Brings Rebirth
. There are also many methods of single-minded recitation in the Pure Land canon, all of which may be used. In addition, I recommend that you read
Habit and Success
Do away with the bad habit of distracted recitation, cultivate the good habit of single-minded recitation, and let habit become nature
(habit becomes nature)
—success or failure hangs on this very step

Here, this author sincerely wishes: may centers of single-minded recitation blossom everywhere. There, the teaching masters wholeheartedly transmit single-minded recitation and guide it with care and effectiveness; the learners recite single-mindedly with warm sincerity and persevere single-mindedly without pause. They learn from one another, help one another, encourage one another, urge one another on, and exchange experience and insight. This is the field where Buddhas are chosen; with a single mind you pass the exam and return
—let us meet in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss!
[Passing the examination.] Being selected by passing an examination.
Further reading:
This Life Is My Last in the Saha World (read aloud)
